claims.text: This is a single-counter yakitori omakase where every skewer is grilled on the same shared binchotan hearth. Both salt and tare (a wheat-containing soy-based sauce) skewers come off the same grill, so cross-contact is effectively unavoidable. Gluten-free cannot be assured and the meal is not celiac-safe.

The set is a fixed omakase that moves cut by cut through the bird and finishes with rice bowls such as soboro-don and oyakodon, leaving little room to remove gluten-containing components without unraveling the course.

Many skewers and the finishing rice bowls are seasoned with tare and soy-based sauces; standard Japanese soy sauce and yakitori tare contain wheat. The omakase leans on these soy- and dashi-based seasonings throughout.

This is a dedicated chicken restaurant; the omakase is built around chicken skewers, chicken soup, and egg-and-chicken rice bowls, with vegetables grilled on the same chicken-fat-coated grill. There is no vegan or vegetarian path through the course.

name: alt. coffee roasters（オルト コーヒー ロースターズ） (alt. coffee roasters)

claims.text: No published information on flour/wheat cross-contamination in the kitchen; gluten-containing items (e.g. bagel sandwiches) are made on-site alongside GF sweets, so a strict GF diner should confirm specific items with staff.
The Nijo/Nakagyo kitchen is fully plant-based with no milk, eggs or dairy used, which greatly reduces the risk of animal-product cross-contact.
Cow's milk was eliminated and replaced with organic oat milk for all drinks, so even lattes and desserts are dairy-free.
The shop asks guests to tell staff about vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies before ordering so a suitable item can be chosen.
Staff speak English, making it easier for foreign visitors to discuss ingredients and allergies.
Entirely vegan menu run by a nutritionist owner, with sweets made without white sugar using amazake, brown sugar and fermented seasonings.
Gluten-free options are available, with several cakes and ice cream noted as gluten-free.

name: アラシのキッチン (Arash's Kitchen)

claims.text: Kitchen prepares naan and other wheat-based items alongside dishes; no dedicated gluten-free preparation or fryer is documented, so cross-contact is likely. Celiac guests should confirm directly.

This is a Halal omnivore kitchen cooking meat kababs and curries; vegan dishes are made in the same kitchen, so shared-surface/utensil contact with meat and dairy is possible. Some 'vegetarian' items contain dairy (paneer, yogurt, cheese) — confirm vegan vs vegetarian per dish.
The restaurant publicly states it accommodates vegetarian, egg-free and dairy-free diners and invites guests to contact them about dietary needs by phone or email.
Wide selection of naturally plant-based mezze and mains (falafel, hummus, baba ghanoush, salad shirazi, dal, and several Persian rice dishes) makes a satisfying vegan meal feasible.
Halal kitchen with no pork on premises and explicit willingness to prepare egg-free and dairy-free dishes.

name: asian chample foods goya（アジアンチャンプルフーズ ゴヤ） (Asian Chample Foods Goya)

claims.text: No information is published on whether the soy sauce used is wheat-free; standard Japanese shoyu typically contains wheat. Confirm directly if avoiding gluten.
Meat-based Okinawan dishes are prepared in the same kitchen, so a fully vegan order should be requested explicitly.
Staff routinely ask diners whether cheese, egg or dashi are acceptable, showing solid awareness of vegan and vegetarian dietary needs when taking orders.
English-speaking staff and an English menu make it easier to communicate dietary restrictions.
Vegan dishes are clearly marked on the menu, so plant-based diners can choose confidently.
Staff proactively confirm dashi/egg/cheese, which is a strong allergy-awareness signal for an omnivore restaurant.

The kitchen is a working Italian restaurant centered on wood-fired pizza and pasta, so wheat flour is in heavy use; a gluten-free menu is offered but no dedicated gluten-free prep area or fryer is published, so cross-contamination cannot be ruled out without asking.
da Maeda is not a fully-plant-based kitchen — meat/animal dishes are prepared alongside the vegan menu, so vegan diners should state their requirements clearly when ordering.
The restaurant explicitly asks guests to tell staff about vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies before choosing a dish, and offers English staff and menus to help.
Vegetables are organic and largely from the chef-owner's own farm in Nantan, Kyoto, and clearly-marked vegan and vegetarian options are part of the standard menu.
For fully-vegan diners, the same owner runs Lapis at this address — a 100%-vegan sushi kaiseki (reservation only) with gluten-free options on most menus, eliminating animal cross-contact.

name: 本と野菜 OyOy (Hon to Yasai OyOy (Book and Vege OyOy))

claims.text: The entire kitchen is vegetarian with no meat or fish, so there is no animal-protein cross-contact from meat or seafood; the main risk for vegans is dairy and egg used in some desserts and light items, not shared cooking surfaces with meat.
Fully vegetarian kitchen using organic, pesticide-free seasonal vegetables from partner farms, with a clearly designated all-plant-based vegetable plate for vegans.
Reviewers praise the vegan platter's many distinct vegetable preparations as a highlight, in a calm bookstore setting with soft jazz.

name: ikuri café（イクリカフェ） (ikuri café)

claims.text: 100% buckwheat (Dattan) soba is naturally gluten-free, but brown rice udon on the same menu contains wheat (about 30% brown-rice flour mixed with wheat), and no separate cooking water or GF protocol is documented — likely shared boiling water between wheat and non-wheat noodles.
A wheat-free plant-based soy sauce option is offered to accompany the buckwheat noodles, but it is not confirmed to be used throughout the kitchen.
Kitchen is 100% plant-based, so there is no meat, fish, egg or dairy cross-contact; no fish dashi is used (kombu/kelp broth only).
The kitchen accommodates 五葷抜き (omitting the five pungent alliums) on request, indicating willingness to adapt for dietary needs, though no formal allergy protocol is stated.
Entirely plant-based, whole-foods menu with no artificial ingredients or additives — every dish is vegan, removing all animal-product cross-contact risk.
Soups use kombu (kelp) dashi only, with no hidden fish stock.

name: いただき繕 京都西陣店 (Itadakizen Kyoto (Itadaki Zen Kyoto Nish)

claims.text: Not a dedicated gluten-free kitchen in Kyoto; fried items share oil, so fried dishes are not celiac-safe even when a gluten-free version of an item exists.
Wheat content of soy sauce/seasonings is not confirmed in available sources; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so a strict GF diner should ask whether wheat-free tamari is used.
The entire kitchen is fully vegan (no animal products, dairy or eggs used), so there is no animal cross-contact — a strong positive for vegan diners.
Staff are described as accommodating to allergies; notify them in advance, ideally when booking online, and confirm specifics directly.
100% plant-based kitchen using organic, pesticide-free, locally sourced vegetables and house-made fermented ingredients — no risk of hidden fish dashi or animal stock.
Tofu steak can be prepared gluten-free, and some items have a gluten-free option, so GF-flexible diners have safe choices when staff are informed.
